forces: Boy soprano, string quartet, harp and organ
performers: Alain Fauqueur, boy soprano; J. J. Grunenwald, organ; members of the Orchestre des Concerts Lamoureux; Igor Markevitch, conductor
intro: Alain Fauqueur’s boy soprano sings Boulanger’s last completed work, a prayer surrounded by restless organ chords and four solo strings. The harp waits until the closing pages, where the music finds G major.

sections.label: A · Voice above chromatic organ
sections.mNote: The organ moves in semitones beneath long vocal notes

sections.label: B · Organ and strings alone
sections.mNote: The singer rests while the organ and strings climb

sections.label: C · The quiet voice returns
sections.mNote: A plaintive vocal line over repeated organ pedal notes

sections.label: D · Harp and muted strings
sections.mNote: Harp and muted strings carry the prayer towards G major

cues.title: Semitones beneath the prayer
cues.text: The organ’s paired notes creep up and down by semitones. Above them, the strings hold their notes and the voice stretches the Latin prayer into long phrases. The harp has nothing to play yet.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, plate D. & F. 10086 (1922), pp. 2–3: Assez lent, chromatic organ writing, sustained strings and vocal line; harp rests. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/bf/IMSLP230262-SIBLEY1802.21472.93de-39087015816665score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nadia takes the dictation
cues.text: In 1918 Lili is too ill to write the notes herself. From her bed she dictates Pie Jesu to Nadia, her elder sister. It is her last completed work.
cues.evidence: Konstantin Galluhn, preface to Vieille prière bouddhique (Musikproduktion Höflich, 2010), describes the dictation of Pie Jesu from Boulanger’s sickbed. https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/987.html

cues.title: The organ grows
cues.text: With the singer silent, the organ takes the chromatic figure into both hands. Boulanger asks the player to add stops little by little. The string lines climb with it, and the score insists on Sans presser — without hurrying.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1922), p. 4, figure 2: vocal rests, expanding organ registration, string crescendo and Sans presser.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A plaintive voice
cues.text: The voice returns pianissimo, marked plaintif. Underneath, the organ pedal repeats the same low note while the upper chords shift. Little string solos enter around the singer: first viola, then second violin and cello.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1922), pp. 4–5: plaintif vocal return, repeated organ pedal and successive solo string entries before figure 3.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A boy’s voice
cues.text: A boy sings this prayer. The Everest sleeve names the soloist as Alain Fauqueur of the Petits Chanteurs de Vincennes, and David Noakes’s note on the sleeve hears in the music “ineffable serenity” at the composer’s last hour.
cues.evidence: Everest LPBR 6059 (1960), sleeve: roster credit and David Noakes’s note on Pie Jesu. https://archive.org/details/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d

cues.title: The waiting harp
cues.text: The harp finally joins in. Boulanger marks the strings muted and the tempo Lent; the voice is calm and clear. Chromatic notes still pass through the accompaniment, but the final Amen settles over a low G, and the last chord is G major.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1922), pp. 6–7, figure 4 to the end: Lent, harp entry, muted strings, Amen and final G-major chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nadia’s lifelong ambition
cues.text: Lili dies at Mézy-sur-Seine on 15 March 1918, aged twenty-four. Forty-two years later Everest issues this record, and its sleeve says it had been Nadia’s “lifelong ambition” to have her younger sister’s music recorded.
cues.evidence: Everest LPBR 6059 (1960), sleeve text: https://archive.org/download/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d_djvu.txt. Death at Mézy on 15 March 1918: Konstantin Galluhn’s preface, https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/987.html

transitions.title: The organ takes both lines
transitions.how: At figure 2 the singer rests. The organ’s chromatic figure spreads into both hands above long pedal notes, and the strings climb through a crescendo. Boulanger gradually adds organ stops, then writes Sans presser: the G-minor prayer swells without a faster beat.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score (1922), p. 4, figure 2: vocal rests, organ registration instructions, rising string parts and Sans presser.

transitions.title: One quiet voice
transitions.how: The strings cut off after their forceful chord. The organ drops to pianissimo, its pedal beating a repeated low note beneath held, shifting chords. The voice resumes with Pie Jesu, marked plaintif; the viola and other strings return one at a time.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score (1922), pp. 4–5: final instrumental chord, pianissimo organ, plaintif vocal return and solo string entries.

transitions.title: G major, with harp
transitions.how: A long ritardando leads to Lent and a new, one-sharp key signature. The harp enters, the strings put on mutes, and the organ holds a low G. Semitones still pass through the upper parts; G major becomes fully clear in the final Amen.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score (1922), pp. 6–7: Rit. molto, figure 4 (Lent), harp entry, muted strings, G pedal and final G-major chord.

source.title: Lili Boulanger, Pie Jesu, Durand full score, plate D. & F. 10086
source.locator: Printed pp. 2–7. The string parts are for two violins, viola and cello. The harp enters at figure 4, alongside the muted strings.

timeline.note: The organ moves in semitones beneath held string notes. The harp rests.
The voice enters over the organ’s moving line and sustained strings.
The strings fall silent at figure 1. The organ’s running notes continue beneath the voice.
The singer rests at figure 2 while organ and strings carry the phrase.
The voice returns quietly, marked plaintif, over the organ’s repeated pedal note.
The string quartet returns around the voice as the organ’s chords grow more insistent.
Harp and muted strings join the voice at figure 4. Their final G major chord outlasts the singer.

composer.epithet: At nineteen she won the Prix de Rome; before her death at twenty-four she had written songs of lost love and psalms that shake the room.
facts: Ernest and Raïssa Boulanger’s younger daughter; Nadia’s sister
Paul Vidal for composition; Georges Caussade for counterpoint; Nadia at home
First woman to win the Premier Grand Prix de Rome in composition, 1913
Songs, psalms, chamber and orchestral music; unfinished opera La Princesse Maleine
composer.background:
At the Château de Compiègne in May 1913, five young composers were shut away writing a cantata about Faust and Helen of Troy. Someone had sent champagne. Their joint letter of thanks to the composer Fernand Halphen, dated 31 May and written out by Claude Delvincourt, called them “your young colleagues imprisoned in the château to sing the loves of Faust and Helen”. Among the signatures was Lili Boulanger’s. She was nineteen, and this was her second attempt at the Prix de Rome. Illness had forced her to withdraw the previous year.

In July she became the first woman to win the Premier Grand Prix for musical composition. Thirty-one of the Académie des Beaux-Arts’ thirty-six voters supported her. Faust et Hélène gave them a tenor in love with a woman summoned from antiquity, a mezzo-soprano Helen and a baritone devil, all carried by a substantial orchestra. The compulsory text was Eugène Adenis’s adaptation of Goethe. Lili dedicated the score to Nadia, who had won a second prize in 1908.
